sweep_summary: search for vene1258 (Venetian, catalog = lexical on the 1995 Grafia Veneta Unitaria manual). The single works with stress in the title, Guzzo & Garcia 2020 (Journal of Language Contact 13(2): 389-427), was obtained as the authors' accepted-manuscript preprint from OSF (osf.io/r8gup; the Brill CC BY-NC PDF is behind an AWS WAF captcha for scripts) and read in full: it concerns variable vowel reduction in clitic se in the Brazilian Portuguese of the Italian Immigration Area and the prosodic domains of clitic types; Veneto (IIA-Veneto and Northern-Italy Veneto alike) appears only as the contact language whose clitic and word-final upper-mid vowels are not reduced and whose clitics undergo juncture — it says nothing about word-stress placement, so it is silent on the catalog's classification (relevance: prosody but not word stress). Bibliographic correction: the DOI attached to this entry in Glottolog (10.1177/0267658319882457) is wrong — Crossref resolves it to Garcia 2019 'Language transfer and positional bias in English stress' (Second Language Research); the real DOI is 10.1163/19552629-bja10021. Beyond the works with stress in the title, our files already held (downloaded 2026-09-16) Guzzo 2023 JIPA 'Brazilian Veneto (Talian)' and Guzzo 2024 Languages 9:259, both re-read: they give the best first-hand phonological stress statements for the Talian dialect (tali1266 under vene1258) — a right-edge trisyllabic window, penultimate default, final stress when the last syllable is CVC ('almost exceptionless'), contrastive stress (méscola/mescola/mescolà) with antepenultimate and final-CV stress as orthographically marked lexical exceptions, cued by duration and vowel quality rather than f0/intensity. A newly downloaded LSRL 2021 handout (Garcia & Guzzo) adds that Central Veneto of Italy shares the trisyllabic window. These confirm and refine the catalog's lexical classification and its orthographic default rule but describe the Brazilian heritage variety, so they do not supersede the GVU manual as the deciding source for Venetian of Italy; a phonologist's statement for Italy-Veneto (Zamboni 1974; Lepschy 1963 word, still could not be reached by automated download; Canepari 1976 JIPA, paywalled) remains the open gap.

new_statements.quote: Stress assignment falls within a trisyllabic window from right to left, as typically observed in Romance languages (Roca 1999). In other words, stress may fall on the final (/pu»pa/ pupa ‘daddy’), penultimate (/»vaka/ vaca ‘cow’) or antepenultimate syllable (/»pjegoRa/ piegora ‘sheep’). The most frequent stress position is penultimate. Word-final heavy syllables (i.e. word-final syllables that end in a coda) seem to attract stress (e.g. /fo»goN/ fogon ‘stove’, /su»doR/ sudor ‘sweat’, and /ka»pEl/ capel ‘hat’). Stress is contrastive in Talian, as illustrated by the triad in (3).

new_statements.reading: Lexical (contrastive) word stress confined to the last three syllables, penultimate as the commonest position, with a stated tendency for a final closed syllable to attract stress; Guzzo 2024 (same author, same variety) sharpens this to 'penultimate unless the final syllable is CVC, then final; almost exceptionless', with antepenultimate and final-CV stress as orthographically marked lexical exceptions. This agrees with the catalog's lexical classification and its orthographic default (the secondary-stress rule), and adds a first-hand phonologist's statement plus a weight tendency the GVU manual does not make. Caveat: the variety described is Talian/Brazilian Veneto (Glottolog dialect tali1266 under vene1258, a Veneto-based koine close to Central Veneto), not Veneto of Italy; the window is stated as trisyllabic, whereas the GVU manual admits bisdrucciole (fourth-from-last) for Italian Veneto.

new_statements.quote: Apocope occurs if -l, -n or -r is preceded by the vowels -a, -e and -i, which results in stress on the last syllable. If the final vowels were not deleted, the stress would be on the penultimate sylable. bŏnŭ(m) > /boŋ/, *frātĕllu(m) > /fra'del/, vĭdēre > /'veder/, afitual /afitu'al/, canocial /kano'ćal/, dental /den'tal/ [...] Apocope does not occur if -l is preceded by -o, allowing stress to fall (generally) on first syllable, or in some cases on antepenult: amolo /'amolo/, bacolo /'bakolo/, bugnigolo /bu'ɲigolo/ [...] In nouns where -n historically preceded final vowel which was lost, stress generally falls on the last syllable [...] Final vowels preceded by -r are generally affected by apocope, which places the stress on the last syllable
new_statements.citation: Rosic, Durda Bosiljka (2002). Linguistic Identity of the Dialect of Fiume. Univ. University of Toronto. 401 pp.
new_statements.locator: Thesis pp. 78-79 (PDF pp. 91-92), section 2.3.17 'Phonological Processes', 1(c) 'Apocope' (verified against the page images); supporting remarks thesis p. 54 (PDF 67, stress diacritics in dialect writing), p. 136 (PDF 149, -u loanwords 'are stressed'), p. 382 (PDF 392, symbol table: ' = primary stress). The thesis has no dedicated stress/accent section; chapter 2 'Phonology' (pp. 52-124) is a historical vowel/consonant treatment.
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's lexical classification and with Guzzo 2023/2024 (penultimate default, final stress when the final syllable is closed, antepenultimate as a lexical class): Rosic's Fiuman data show the same three-way distribution and add the diachronic mechanism (apocope of final vowels after -l/-n/-r moves stress to the final syllable) plus the -olo antepenultimate class and stressed -u loanwords. She never states a synchronic rule, a trisyllabic window, or anything on secondary stress. The variety is Fiuman (Rijeka/Fiume, Croatia), a colonial eastern-Venetan dialect, not Veneto of Italy or Brazilian Talian.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Rosic gives no synchronic stress rule; stress is marked with a primary-stress tick in every phonemic transcription (symbol table p. 382) and she notes (p. 54) that dialect orthography marks stress on unexpected syllables. The placement that emerges from her apocope section is the Romance three-way picture: words that keep a final vowel are stressed on the penultimate ('the stress would be on the penultimate syllable' if the final vowel had not been deleted); consonant-final words produced by apocope of -Vl/-Vn/-Vr are stressed on the final syllable (fra'del, kan'ton, kali'ger, and loanwords fur'gon, vah'ter, and -u loans bisu, paspartu, p. 136); the -olo class (amolo, bakolo, nuvolo, refolo, rodolo, bu'ɲigolo) is stressed on the first or antepenultimate syllable. In effect: penultimate default, final stress in closed final syllables, antepenultimate in a lexical class, all inside a three-syllable window, i.e. lexical stress with a strong weight tendency.
new_statements.exceptions: Vowel-final words that escaped apocope keep penultimate/antepenultimate stress: afano /a'fano/, lavrano /'lavrano/; mistro /'mistro/, polastro /po'lastro/, zucaro /'tsukaro/; loanwords boro, muro, sbiro, tabaro, timbro, zilindro /tsi'lindro/ (p. 79-80). Verb infinitives movēre, vidēre shifted stress to the first syllable ('mover, 'veder, p. 58); 'ampola < ampulla shows a stress shift to the first syllable (p. 66); nouns in -u (bisu < bijou, paspartu) 'are assimilated loanwords and are stressed' (p. 136).
new_statements.identity_note: Rosic 2002 describes Fiuman (el dialeto fiuman), the Venetian-type dialect of Rijeka/Fiume, Croatia, which she classifies as a colonial eastern-Venetan variety (apocope pattern shared with Venezia, Caorle, Chioggia); data from a 1997 ALI-style questionnaire given to Italian-school students in Rijeka plus older descriptions (Bató, Il dialetto di Fiume). The PuRe record tags it ISO 639-3 vec; it is a dialect under vene1258, not Veneto of Italy and not Brazilian Talian (tali1266), the variety behind the existing Guzzo statements. Fiuman has a five-vowel system without the open/closed mid-vowel contrast of other Venetan dialects and residual vowel-length contrasts (p. 53), which Rosic notes but does not connect to stress.

Stress is mostly penultimate, unless the final syllable is CVC, in which case stress is final (Guzzo 2023). sources.quote: The Veneto data that are discussed in this section apply both to IIA-Veneto and the Veneto varieties spoken in Northern Italy. ... neither pronominal nor non-pronominal clitics exhibiting an upper-mid vowel undergo vowel reduction (e.g., Zamboni, 1974; Frosi and Mioranza, 1983), as the examples in (18) show. ... In the case of final upper-mid vowels, raising to high implies a difference in meaning, as word-final morpheme -i is used to signal pluralization in masculine nouns (Zamboni, 1974; Frosi and Mioranza, 1983; see also Walker, 2005)
